I don't think the climate change fight is one that is worth fighting. We live on a living planet, of course the climate is changing. It changes all of the time. Of course humans are influencing it. I'm libertarian, but I also believe that this statement couldn't be more wrong. Climate change is perhaps one of the biggest issues that we will be facing in the future.

Climate change is expected to have a serious impact on food production, which could potentially double food prices as early as 2050.

Sea level rise, though not the doomsday scenario that climate alarmists say it is, will cause serious problems in the form of storm surge, which will damage our infrastructure as was seen in Hurricane Sandy (hurricane Sandy caused $68B in damage).

The severity of extreme weather events, such as hurricanes, is expected to be on average more severe in the future, increasing the monetary cost of such events. To put it in perspective, Hurricane Katrina did $500M in damage to Keesler Air Force Base, which should put into perspective just how costly a single event can be for the American taxpayer.

None of these direct impacts of climate change are the most serious though, the most serious are the indirect effects of climate change. Climate change is a threat multiplier, making areas that are already turbulent more likely to have even more problems. Drought, which impacts food production, is a perfect example. ISIS was born out of a civil conflict which began as a result of food shortages in Syria, which were the result of a drought. A recent study discovered that the drought was made 2-3 times more likely from the current level of warming (only 0.85C of the expected unavoidable 2C).

Did climate change cause ISIS? Of course not. But do we expect to see areas that are extremely vulnerable to climate change have an increased rate of conflict? Absolutely. And those conflicts fuel the flow of refugees. Just look at what's happening in Europe right now as a result of refugees fleeing conflict, and now think about how much worse it will be when Sub-Saharan Africa (one of the most vulnerable parts of the world) suffers the worst effects of climate change.

These refugees and subsequent conflicts have an effect on our foreign policy interests, which I need not remind anyone here are rooted in economic interests. Why do we care what happens in the Middle East? Because it affects energy prices in the U.S. Why do we care if hurricanes ravage the Caribbean? Because most of those refugees are going to try to come to the US. Why do we care if crop yields decline? Because food prices have a major role in the US economy.

I'm libertarian, I'm opposed to needless government intervention which weakens us and inhibits the freedoms of others. However, I'm not ignorant. I know that there is an overwhelming scientific consensus showing us that climate change is a HUGE problem, which will have far reaching consequences. It is a collective action problem though, which means that it's important for even libertarians to understand that it requires a collective solution.

In my mind climate change is one of those problems that's in the same category as national defense, or making sure road rules are the same everywhere. It's a problem where actors who defect on the system create a situation that is unsustainable.

With all that said though, I think it's important for everyone to also recognize that climate change is an economic problem. We're going to pay for the effects of climate change, one way or another. The question is do we wait until our economy is ravaged and we're too weak to do anything, or do we make some investments now to prevent the worst case scenarios? Personally I'm of a mind that the minimal investment is worth it to make sure that myself and my progeny will enjoy the same level of economic freedom and prosperity that my ancestors have.

And for the record, I have professional experience in energy and climate security research.

This book is too heavy to read while in bed. It is too intense to read without paying full attention. It is too dense to be read in less than 1hr runs.

You seem to be describing the fundamental issue with more scientific books, one I face myself as well. It's simply incredibly hard to get into them without an ulterior driving motive, isn't it?

For myself, I do two things that seem to help quite a lot, as I too am a sporadic reader:

  • Read many of these books at a time

  • Take notes that are to be briefly perused before starting again.

The first one seems rather unintuitive, but it's mostly a measure against getting bored. The second serves two purposes: To keep the mind engaged while reading, and to remind the mind when starting again.

Good luck! Do try to have fun.

I made an effort to read GEB on weekends, when I could play music, sit at the kitchen table, have a coffee/tea ready, and knew I had the ability for the "1hr run" at minimum.

If you're not feeling it, there are probably other non-fiction books that can be digested in easier chunks, are "lighter" in terms of both content, and physical copies. That is okay. The book isn't going to feel neglected, anyone who judges you for not having enough time at the moment hasn't gone through something similar. You can come back to it when you have some time off, if the mood strikes.
